claims.text: ProductsController.List() has a single return, Ok(products), with no branch on how many rows the query returned; it answers 200 regardless of the row count, including zero.
ProductsController.Get(int id) calls db.Products.FindAsync(id); if the result is null it returns NotFound() (404) before building any ProductDto, otherwise it returns Ok(new ProductDto(...)) (200).
Neither List() nor Get(int id) in ProductsController writes to the database; both only read via db.Products.

Sending GET /api/v1/products/1 to the running stage-1 lab returns 200 with one product's JSON; sending GET /api/v1/products/999999 returns 404 with a problem+json body carrying no product data; sending GET /api/v1/products returns 200 with a JSON array of the seeded products.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang stage-1 lab: curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1, /api/v1/products/999999, and /api/v1/products; db/seed.sql at tag stage-1

claims.text: By HTTP convention GET is a safe method: the client does not request and does not expect any change to the resource, and safe methods are also idempotent, so safe is the stronger of the two promises.

A collection GET stays 200 whatever the row count: an empty set is still a representation of the (existing) collection, so row count never turns the answer into a 404. A URL naming no collection at all is a different case.
claims.source_hint: REST resource-naming convention, independent of any one framework

claims.text: 404 (Not Found) indicates the server has nothing to return for the target resource; it does not assert that the resource definitively does not exist anywhere (RFC 9110 allows a server to answer 404 even for a resource it declines to disclose).

[HttpGet] on List() maps to GET /api/v1/products; [HttpGet("{id:int}")] on Get(int id) maps to that same prefix followed by an integer (negatives match too), bound to the id parameter; a non-integer segment matches no route at all.
